items.title: The Phases of Transcription and mRNA Processing

source_refs.note: The phases of transcription with both For Information boxes and post-transcriptional modifications (PDF 133-136); Figures 19.13 to 19.16 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: No primer is needed. RNA polymerase binds the template DNA at a special nucleotide sequence, the promoter, which is not itself transcribed.

blocks.caption: Promoter sequences
rows: -35 sequence, about 35 nucleotides before the start point

blocks.alt: A prokaryotic promoter on double-stranded DNA. Coding strand 5' to 3' with TTGACA at the -35 sequence, TATAAT at the -10 sequence and A at the start point; template strand 3' to 5' with the complementary AACTGT, ATATTA and T. A green arrow from 5' to 3' shows the direction of transcription.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.13: Promoters in prokaryotes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.13).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Coding strand, Template strand, -35 sequence, -10 sequence, Start point, Transcription, 5', 3'.

blocks.text: RNA polymerase has five subunits: two alpha subunits bind regulatory proteins, beta prime binds the template DNA, beta binds RNA nucleotides, and sigma recognises the promoter and initiates synthesis. After the enzyme attaches to the promoter the sigma subunit is removed, and the other four, the core enzyme, unwind the helix and break the base pairs, forming the transcription bubble in which the RNA chain is assembled.

blocks.title: For information: RNA polymerases
blocks.text: Prokaryotes have one RNA polymerase, which makes all three kinds of RNA. Eukaryotes have three: RNA polymerase I makes rRNA in the nucleolus, RNA polymerase II makes mRNA and RNA polymerase III makes tRNA.

Inside the bubble RNA polymerase builds a chain of complementary ribonucleotides along the template in the 5' to 3' direction, usually starting with A or G. The nucleotides come as ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs); as each is added two phosphates detach with release of energy. The first 12 bases of the new mRNA form a temporary helix with the template that keeps the 3' end in place to receive the next nucleotide; the RNA-DNA helix rotates as each nucleotide is added, keeping the 3' end at the catalytic site. The bubble moves along the DNA, the growing mRNA protrudes from it, and the DNA re-winds behind.

blocks.alt: A transcription bubble inside a pink RNA polymerase. The DNA ahead is unwinding and the DNA behind is rewinding (curved red arrows). The coding strand (yellow) loops over the top; along the template strand (blue) the new mRNA (orange) forms a short DNA-RNA hybrid helix, its 3' end growing and its 5' end leaving the enzyme. rNTPs enter the polymerase; a green arrow shows the direction of movement.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.14: Elongation phase of transcription (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.14).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Template strand, Coding strand, Rewinding, Unwinding, mRNA, DNA-RNA hybrid helix, rNTPs, RNA polymerase, 5', 3'.

blocks.text: At the end of a gene there is a stop region: a series of G-C base pairs followed by a series of A-T pairs. When it is transcribed, hydrogen bonds form within the mRNA strand, making a loop called the GC hairpin, followed by a tail of four or more U nucleotides. The hairpin makes RNA polymerase pause, and the U-A pairs between the RNA and the DNA, the weakest pairs, cannot hold the RNA-DNA hybrid together during the long pause, so the RNA separates and transcription stops.

blocks.alt: Top: RNA polymerase paused at the stop region of the DNA, the mRNA ending in UUUU paired to the stop region, and a GC hairpin formed in the mRNA behind it; an inset shows the hairpin's sequence, 5' C A then C G G C G C paired with G C C G C G, a loop G G C U U, and the 3' tail U U U U U. Below: the polymerase released, the DNA strands rewound, and the mRNA separated.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.15: Termination phase of transcription (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.15).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Polymerase paused, Stop region, GC hairpin, Polymerase released, DNA strands rewind, mRNA separates, 5', 3'.

blocks.text: Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so their mRNA, made in the cytoplasm, starts translation at once. In eukaryotes the new mRNA must travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and on the way it is modified.

items: 5' cap: the first nucleotide of the mRNA is A or G; a methylated G nucleotide is joined to it by a 5' to 5' bond. The cap protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases on its journey.
3' poly-A tail: a chain of about 250 A nucleotides added at the 3' end, which protects the mRNA from breakdown by nucleases.
Splicing: the new mRNA contains introns, which do not code for protein, and exons, which are translated. Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons to give mature mRNA.

blocks.alt: Template DNA 3' to 5' with a promoter and four exons separated by three introns; transcription gives the immature mRNA 5' to 3' with the same exons and introns; addition of a 5' cap (GTP) and a 3' poly-A tail (AAAA); mRNA splicing removes the introns and gives the mature mRNA: 5' cap, protein-coding sequence, 3' poly-A tail, ready to move to cytoplasm. A bracket marks the steps after transcription as post-transcriptional modifications.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.16: Post-transcriptional changes in eukaryotes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.16).
